exercises.prompt:
What does this print (Ruby 3.4 or later)?

```ruby
p %w[a b a c b a].tally
```
hints: `tally` counts how often each element occurs.
Hashes keep insertion order: the order in which each value first appeared.
exercises.solution: `tally` returns a hash from each distinct element to its count, in order of first appearance: `{"a" => 3, "b" => 2, "c" => 1}`. (Ruby 3.4 changed `Hash#inspect` to put spaces around `=>`; older versions print `{"a"=>3, …}`.)

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ruby
h = Hash.new([])
h[:x] << 1
p [h[:y], h.size]
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `h[:x]` returned the shared default array, `<<` changed it, and no key was ever assigned.

hints: `Hash.new([])` uses one array object as the default for every missing key.
exercises.solution: `h[:x]` returns the single shared default array, and `<< 1` modifies it. No key is ever stored, so `h.size` is 0. Reading `h[:y]` returns the same (now modified) default: `[1]`. Output: `[[1], 0]`. Use `Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }` instead.


feedback.message: Not yet. That would be `each_slice(2)` (without the leftover 5). `each_cons` makes overlapping pairs.

exercises.solution: `each_cons(2)` yields overlapping pairs: [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [4, 5]. Their products are `[2, 6, 12, 20]`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```ruby
a = [[0]]
b = a.dup
b[0] << 1
b << [2]
p a
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `dup` copies the outer array, but the inner array is shared.
Not yet. Appending `[2]` changed only `b`'s outer array.

hints: Which of the two changes touches an object that `a` also contains?
exercises.solution: `b` is a new outer array containing the *same* inner array as `a`. `b[0] << 1` modifies that shared inner array, so `a` sees it. `b << [2]` changes only `b`. So `a` is `[[0, 1]]`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print?

```ruby
p (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { it * 3 }.select(&:even?).first(3)
```
hints: Keep the even ones, and stop after three.
exercises.solution: The lazy pipeline produces 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, … one at a time, keeps the even ones, and stops once it has three: `[6, 12, 18]`. Without `lazy`, `map` would try to build an infinite array and never finish.
